feed.title: Wits AHEAD · Daily briefing
feed.subtitle: News, research, video and readings on AI, data and human capability in higher education, curated every morning.
feed.rights: Wits AHEAD Research Group, Wits School of Education, University of the Witwatersrand

entry.title: South African universities write their own AI rules as the national department falls behind
entry.summary:
Daily Maverick reports that North-West University, Stellenbosch, the University of Cape Town, Wits and other South African universities have each adopted their own policies or frameworks for artificial intelligence in teaching and assessment, while the Department of Higher Education and Training has yet to issue a national AI policy, citing capacity constraints in its legal services. Parliament's higher education portfolio committee has asked the department for a timeline, and academics quoted in the piece warn that leaving each institution to act alone risks widening inequality between better and less resourced universities.

Why it matters for AHEAD: The gap between fast-moving institutional policy and a still-absent national framework is exactly the governance question at the heart of Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, and it is one the group's own South African context makes hard to ignore.

Daily Maverick · Established press

entry.title: African Union ministers endorse a continental education data portal and 60 CESA indicators
entry.summary:
Ministers at the African Union's sixth Specialized Technical Committee on Education, Science and Technology, meeting in Addis Ababa on 6 November 2026, endorsed 60 standardised indicators aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals for the Continental Education Strategy for Africa 2026 to 2035, and asked the African Union Commission to build a continental digital reporting portal and CESA policy dashboard with UNESCO's Institute for Statistics and the Global Education Monitoring Report. The same session cleared five sectoral artificial intelligence publications for national adaptation and called for parliamentary dialogue and digital literacy on AI governance across the continent.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's fifth pillar, analytics and data for education systems and decision-making, a continent-wide indicators framework and reporting portal is the kind of shared infrastructure that could let African ministries compare progress and target support, provided member states actually resource the rollout.

African Union Commission · Intergovernmental body: African Union communique

entry.title: South African study reframes early warning as early success indicators for student support
entry.summary:
Writing in the Journal of Student Affairs in Africa, Philokuhle Majozi and Kgadi Mathabathe propose a strengths-based framework of 'early success indicators' for a South African university, moving away from deficit language such as 'at-risk' and 'early warning'. Drawing on interviews with academic success coaches, institutional leaders and data scientists, the article maps data points and support touchpoints across the student lifecycle, from pre-registration to final assessment, and argues for a shift from reactive to proactive student support.

Why it matters for AHEAD: The paper speaks directly to Wits AHEAD's second pillar, AI and predictive analytics for student success, and its strengths-based reframing of early warning systems offers South African universities a model that ties data-informed support to dignity rather than deficit.

Journal of Student Affairs in Africa · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: University of Colorado adopts a systemwide policy for the responsible use of AI
entry.summary:
The University of Colorado system has introduced Administrative Policy Statement 6012, Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence, which took effect on 24 August 2026 and applies across its campuses. The policy requires staff, faculty and students to disclose generative AI use that contributes to university decisions, to review AI-generated material for accuracy and bias before relying on it, and keeps confidential information out of unapproved AI tools, alongside existing rules on information security, records and intellectual property.

Why it matters for AHEAD: A major US university system's move to a single, disclosure-based framework for AI use offers a concrete comparator for Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, as it tracks how institutions worldwide are governing AI in teaching, research and decision-making.

University of Colorado · University announcement

entry.title: University of KwaZulu-Natal scholar warns that AI could entrench dysfunction and colonial hierarchies in South African university governance
entry.summary:
Writing in the South African Journal of Higher Education, R. Dhunpath of the University of KwaZulu-Natal argues that South African universities show strikingly similar patterns of institutional dysfunction, which neo-institutional theory explains as 'isomorphism': pressure to adopt similar structures to appear legitimate, rather than to perform well pedagogically. The article extends this argument to artificial intelligence, warning that AI risks embedding these pressures into an 'algorithmic iron cage' governing admissions, assessment and research metrics, and that adopting AI models built on Global North data risks reproducing colonial hierarchies in technical form, which the author calls 'colonial isomorphism 2.0'.

Why it matters for AHEAD: A sharply argued South African critique of how AI could deepen institutional dysfunction and colonial dependency in university governance speaks directly to Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, and to its attentiveness to Global South perspectives on AI adoption.

South African Journal of Higher Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: UCT video marks Africa's first Times Higher Education World Academic Summit, held under the banner of AI and justice
entry.summary:
The University of Cape Town has released a video marking its hosting, with the University of Bristol, of the Times Higher Education World Academic Summit in Cape Town from 29 September to 1 October 2026, the first time the summit has been held on African soil. Under the theme 'Knowledge, justice and futures: universities in the age of intelligence', the three-day gathering brought together university leaders, researchers and policymakers from around the world to debate artificial intelligence, inequality and the future purpose of higher education.

Why it matters for AHEAD: A global summit choosing Cape Town, and African universities helping set its agenda on AI and justice, speaks directly to Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, and to its mission of advancing human capability in higher education across the Global South.

University of Cape Town · University video

entry.title: Study of 162 Ugandan undergraduates finds generative AI lifts fluency but can erode originality
entry.summary:
A study of 162 undergraduates at Victoria University in Kampala, Uganda, found that using ChatGPT significantly increased students' fluency and elaboration on a standard divergent-thinking test, but reduced originality among Humanities and Business students, while Science, Technology and Health students showed no significant change. Copying AI output directly predicted lower originality, while revising it through repeated prompting predicted higher originality, the peer-reviewed study found.

Why it matters for AHEAD: How students use generative AI, not simply whether they use it, emerges as the decisive factor for original thinking, a finding that speaks directly to Wits AHEAD's first pillar, generative AI in higher education: teaching, assessment and integrity, for universities across the Global South.

Journal of Research Innovation and Implications in Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: UNESCO webinar on assessment in the AI era features a Cape Town scholar's call for critical AI literacy
entry.summary:
UNESCO's International Institute for Information Technologies in Education (IITE) and Shanghai Open University hosted a webinar on assessment in higher education in the era of AI and digital technologies, bringing together Dr Christian M. Stracke of the University of Bonn, Professor Juvy Lizette M. Gervacio of the University of the Philippines Open University, and Professor Daniela Gachago of the University of Cape Town. Gachago's keynote argued that pedagogy and design for assessment must centre equity, inclusion and critical AI literacy, alongside the other speakers' focus on sustainable assessment policy and changing assessment strategies.

Why it matters for AHEAD: A South African voice shaping a global conversation on assessment in the AI era speaks directly to Wits AHEAD's first pillar, generative AI in higher education: teaching, assessment and integrity, and its sixth, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy.

UNESCO IITE · Intergovernmental body webinar recording

entry.title: Vaal University of Technology study finds lecturers want clearer AI rules, not bans
entry.summary:
A qualitative study presented by Vaal University of Technology researcher Naledi Kaeane at an international conference in Victoria Falls finds that lecturers at a South African university of technology are already using AI tools in teaching and assessment, but face unclear institutional guidance on accountability and ethical boundaries. Most lecturers see AI as a way to improve efficiency and feedback rather than a threat, and the study recommends clear policy and training over outright bans.

Why it matters for AHEAD: It is a timely, ground-level complement to Wits AHEAD's first pillar, generative AI in higher education, showing why policy clarity, not prohibition, is what South African lecturers say they actually need.

ITWeb (reporting a Vaal University of Technology study) · Established press report on university research

entry.title: Study of 541 pre-service STEM teachers in Lagos finds understanding of AI predicts its classroom use
entry.summary:
A peer-reviewed study of 541 pre-service STEM teachers in Lagos State, Nigeria, finds that how well trainee teachers understand artificial intelligence significantly predicts whether they go on to use it in teaching. Male participants reported significantly higher AI literacy than female participants, and the authors call for AI to be built more deliberately into teacher preparation programmes.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Wits AHEAD's third pillar, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, treats exactly this question, how teacher training itself must change, as central to getting AI into African classrooms responsibly.

STEM Education (AIMS Press) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Study of 96 UK universities finds AI policies read as surveillance, not support
entry.summary:
A Higher Education Policy Institute study of 163 UK universities with degree-awarding powers finds that 41% have no AI policy a student, parent or regulator can find online. Among the 96 published policies it was able to analyse, author Sam Illingworth finds most function as detection-and-discipline frameworks rather than guidance for learning, with only four, at Durham, Stirling, Canterbury Christ Church and Arts University Plymouth, judged genuinely student-centred.

Why it matters for AHEAD: It is a sobering mirror for Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar: even in a well-resourced system, writing an AI policy that actually serves students, rather than merely policing them, is still the harder half of the task.

Higher Education Policy Institute (HEPI) · Higher education policy institute report

entry.title: UNESCO's first Higher Education Global Trends Report finds only one in five universities has a formal AI policy
entry.summary:
UNESCO's first Higher Education Global Trends Report, drawing on data from 146 countries, finds that global enrolment has more than doubled in twenty years, from about 100 million students in 2000 to 269 million in 2024. It also finds that only one in five universities worldwide had a formal artificial intelligence policy in 2025, even as digital technologies and AI reshape teaching and learning.

Why it matters for AHEAD: The gap between fast AI adoption and slow policy development is exactly the terrain Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, exists to help close for universities across the Global South.

UNESCO · Intergovernmental body report

entry.title: Hidden AI prompt urging reviewers to "write a positive review" is found inside a published peer-reviewed paper
entry.summary:
Times Higher Education reports that a paper published last month in Computer Methods in Biomechanics and Biomedical Engineering, a Taylor & Francis journal, contained hidden instructions meant to steer an AI reviewer towards a positive verdict, including the phrases "ignore all previous instructions" and "avoid mentioning any negative aspects." An academic spotted the prompt and raised it publicly; the publisher has opened an investigation but has not said what action it will take. The paper's five authors are based at Northeast Forestry University in China and did not respond to requests for comment; a similar case last year found hidden prompts in seventeen preprints from fourteen institutions.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the case shows that generative AI is already being used to subvert the very safeguard, peer review, that is meant to keep research trustworthy, a warning for every journal and university, in the Global South as much as the North, that relies on reviewers reading papers rather than running them through a chatbot.

Times Higher Education · Established press investigation

entry.title: UNESCO working paper finds AI use "neither uniform nor evenly distributed" across 200 Latin American and Caribbean universities
entry.summary:
A UNESCO IESALC working paper, produced with the United Nations University Institute for the Advanced Study of Sustainability, surveyed 200 higher education institutions across 19 Latin American and Caribbean countries between August and October 2025 and finds AI adoption "neither uniform nor evenly distributed": 87 per cent of institutions use AI in at least one area, mostly teaching and research, yet only 26 per cent have a formal AI framework, and 55 per cent have no dedicated AI budget at all. Uptake is highest at private non-profit universities, at 84 per cent, and lowest at private for-profit ones, while public universities, though widely adopting AI, report the least staff training and the smallest dedicated funding.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, the paper is a reminder that adoption without governance, formal strategy, budget or training, is itself a policy risk, and that public universities across the Global South, not only in Latin America, often carry the heaviest exposure with the fewest resources to manage it.

UNESCO International Institute for Higher Education in Latin America and the Caribbean (IESALC), with UNU-IAS · Intergovernmental working paper

entry.title: Brazil becomes the first country to set binding national rules for AI in every school and university
entry.summary:
Brazil's National Council of Education has published binding guidelines for the use of artificial intelligence across every level of Brazilian education, public and private, taking effect on publication in the official gazette on 12 November 2026. The rules require institutions to adopt their own AI governance policies with documented oversight, ban AI platforms from grading essays or written exams without a qualified human reviewing the full submission, and prohibit any decision affecting a student's rights or academic progress being made by AI alone. Institutions have twelve months to bring their policies, contracts and practices into line, though the ban on fully automated decisions takes effect immediately.

Why it matters for AHEAD: As the first binding national rule of its kind covering an entire higher education system, this gives Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, a concrete, operational model, risk tiers, human oversight and a transition period, that a Global South regulator can adapt rather than build from nothing.

National Council of Education (Conselho Nacional de Educação), Brazil · Government gazette, national regulatory body

entry.title: UK regulator and sector body find AI already undermines the credibility of unsupervised assessment
entry.summary:
A joint study by England's Office for Students and the sector body Advance HE, drawing on conversations with more than 300 students and staff across over 120 institutions between June and September 2026, finds that generative AI helps many students explain difficult concepts, summarise material and revise, but poses a significant risk to unsupervised assessment: in exams and assignments without supervision, students can often produce high-standard work with AI without demonstrating the knowledge intended, and detection tools do not reliably catch it. The report says many students are unclear what AI use their institution permits, and some universities have responded by shifting towards closed-book exams and other supervised formats.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's first pillar, generative AI in higher education, the report is a clear warning that assessment design, not policing AI use after the fact, is what protects the value of a degree, a lesson as relevant to universities in the Global South as to England's.

Office for Students and Advance HE · Report, national regulator and sector body

entry.title: South African scholar warns generative AI risks erasing Indigenous knowledge from African university curricula
entry.summary:
A conceptual paper by Kehdinga George Fomunyam of the Durban University of Technology, published in Trends in Higher Education, argues that large language models rely on data extraction and linguistic dominance that systematically sideline African Indigenous Knowledge Systems in favour of Western ways of thinking. Reviewing peer-reviewed literature and policy from 2020 to 2025 in post-#FeesMustFall South African universities, the paper calls this pattern algorithmic colonialism and warns that uncritical use of generative AI in African curricula risks a single machine-generated consensus displacing local, context-specific knowledge.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This speaks directly to Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, by setting out a concrete risk, the sidelining of Indigenous knowledge, and a response, AI sovereignty built on data trusts, African-sourced training feedback and algorithmic literacy, for African universities adopting generative AI.

Trends in Higher Education (MDPI) · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Trinity College's philosophy department bans AI outright in all its courses
entry.summary:
The philosophy department at Trinity College in Hartford, Connecticut has banned students from using artificial intelligence for any purpose in its courses, from summarising readings and brainstorming to help with writing, editing and preparing for oral exams. All six members of the department backed the policy unanimously, arguing that AI works against its core aim of teaching students to think, read, write, reason and act ethically. The department accepts that the ban will be hard to enforce and says its real purpose is to make students examine what the technology gives them and what it takes away.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Most universities are moving the other way, redesigning assessment around AI rather than ruling it out, so this case tests Wits AHEAD's first pillar, generative AI in higher education, by showing how far one discipline will go to protect how it teaches people to think.

Hartford Courant · Established press

entry.title: An Australian law academic warns AI is already thinning out graduate jobs
entry.summary:
An Australian government report found cognitive desk roles, such as accountants, clerks and receptionists, most exposed to AI automation, and the Reserve Bank of Australia has since noted early signs of younger workers struggling in AI-exposed industries. Writing for The Conversation, a Western Sydney University law academic reports that some law firms have already cut graduate roles as AI takes over routine tasks, and cites his own exam research showing AI's average score on university criminal law exams rose from 52.5 per cent in 2023 to 76.3 per cent in 2025, now ahead of the average student. He argues universities should keep teaching core disciplinary knowledge while training students to direct AI, question its answers and improve on its first attempt.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This links directly to Wits AHEAD's fourth pillar, AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, by setting out what a university curriculum needs to change, not just warn about, as AI reshapes entry-level work.

Western Sydney University (The Conversation) · University commentary

entry.title: New analysis of a US student survey finds AI policy gaps worst in the fields most unsettled by AI
entry.summary:
A Kennesaw State University policy report re-analyses the Lumina Foundation-Gallup 2026 survey of 3,801 United States associate and bachelor's degree students, finding that 57 per cent use AI for coursework at least weekly while 53 per cent say their institutions discourage or prohibit it and 52 per cent describe unclear policies. Grouping students by discipline, the report finds weekly AI use highest in business (70 per cent), technology (68 per cent) and engineering (65 per cent), while 71 per cent of vocational students and 70 per cent of technology students have seriously considered changing their major because of AI. The author concludes that institutional policy and training have not kept pace with how unevenly AI is already used, and worried about, across different fields of study.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This speaks to Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, by showing that a one-size-fits-all AI policy misses exactly the fields where students feel most exposed to AI and least supported.

Kennesaw State University, Coles College of Business · University policy report

entry.title: Small Nigerian college dataset finds a random forest model best predicts student dropout risk
entry.summary:
Researchers at Federal College of Education, Gidan Madi, and Sokoto State University in Nigeria built and compared four machine learning models, logistic regression, decision tree, random forest and a neural network, to predict student dropout from a dataset of 250 students at the college. The random forest model was most accurate at 92 per cent, ahead of logistic regression at 90 per cent and the neural network at 88 per cent, while the decision tree model trailed at 84 per cent. The authors note that most dropout-prediction research relies on large datasets that smaller, data-constrained institutions cannot gather, and argue their small-sample approach is more realistic for similar colleges across Nigeria.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This is a direct contribution to Wits AHEAD's second pillar, AI and predictive analytics for student success, retention and early warning, from a part of the Global South where most early-warning research assumes data that colleges simply do not have.

FUDMA Journal of Sciences · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: South African universities write their own AI rules while the national department lags
entry.summary:
South African universities are moving ahead with their own artificial intelligence policies while the Department of Higher Education and Training (DHET) has yet to produce a national framework, Daily Maverick reported on 18 November 2026. North-West University has had an institutional AI policy for more than a year, Stellenbosch is working to an AI Roadmap for 2026 to 2030, and the University of Cape Town, Wits, the University of Johannesburg and Nelson Mandela University have also issued their own guidance. DHET says capacity constraints, particularly in its legal services component, have delayed its own policy, and Parliament's portfolio committee plans to ask for a timeline.

Why it matters for AHEAD: The gap between fast-moving institutional practice and slow national policy is exactly the governance problem Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, tracks across the Global South, and it shows why individual universities cannot wait for government guidance to protect students and staff.

Daily Maverick · Established press

entry.title: National survey finds US teacher-training programmes unevenly prepared for AI
entry.summary:
A national EdWeek Research Center survey of 268 teacher educators at degree-granting colleges and universities, fielded in August and September 2026 and reported on 16 November 2026, finds more than half of teacher-preparation programmes prepare candidates to use AI for generating teaching ideas or assignments, and nearly two-thirds teach digital and AI literacy for school pupils. Most programmes have no stand-alone AI course; 60 per cent of faculty say individual instructors decide whether to include it, and about a third of respondents say colleagues do not support doing so. Fifty-seven per cent cite AI's rapid pace as an obstacle, 68 per cent want ongoing or repeated training, and about a third say they have had none.

Why it matters for AHEAD: Teacher education is one of Wits AHEAD's six pillars, and the survey's finding that AI is reaching teacher-training curricula faster than institutional support or policy can follow is a pattern the group is also tracking in South African and other Global South teacher-education programmes.

EdWeek Research Center / Education Week · Research centre survey report, established education press

entry.title: New framework asks whether universities are actually ready to govern AI, not just willing
entry.summary:
Writing in the Journal of Ethics in Higher Education, Mohamed Hussien Abdelaziz (Ejada Systems, Cairo) introduces Ethical Readiness, a framework distinguishing universities that merely state responsible AI principles from those with the accountability structures, oversight capacity and corrective mechanisms to actually carry them out. The conceptual paper sets out eight governance dimensions and a seven-stage lifecycle, arguing that the real gap in higher education's AI governance is not between stated values and principles but between those principles and institutional preparedness to apply them.

Why it matters for AHEAD: This gives Wits AHEAD's own pillar on responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy a practical checklist for testing whether a university's AI policy, its own or any of the policies reported elsewhere in today's briefing, is backed by real governance capacity and not just a published document.

Journal of Ethics in Higher Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Unisa symposium weighs how AI is reshaping teaching, support and research
entry.summary:
Unisa's 12th Western Cape Academic Development Symposium brought together academics, students and representatives of five institutions, including the University of Cape Town and Stellenbosch University, to discuss how artificial intelligence is reshaping teaching, student support, employability and research. Delegates heard that Unisa's new student-facing chatbot has already resolved many routine enquiries, once left for days, within minutes, cutting staff workload across the university's nine provincial offices.

Why it matters for AHEAD: The symposium's roundtable on future-ready graduates and technology-enhanced teaching speaks directly to Wits AHEAD's first pillar, generative AI in higher education, and to the shared South African task of putting AI to responsible use at scale.

University of South Africa (Unisa) · University announcement

entry.title: University of Alaska regents delay AI policy drafted with Claude after faculty backlash
entry.summary:
The University of Alaska Board of Regents has postponed a vote on its system-wide guidance document, AI Engaged, after faculty objected that an early draft had been written with help from Anthropic's Claude chatbot. The vote now moves to the regents' February meeting, and the university's AI Coordinating Council will meanwhile help each of its three universities draft its own campus-specific policy.

Why it matters for AHEAD: The row shows that artificial intelligence now shapes university governance itself, not only teaching and assessment, and it is a sharp reminder, for Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar on responsible AI, ethics and policy, that institutions must be able to show their own policy was made transparently and with proper human oversight.

Anchorage Daily News · Established press

entry.title: World Bank report finds South Africa's digital skills pipeline mismatched to job demand
entry.summary:
A World Bank report produced with South Africa's Department of Higher Education and Training and the Mastercard Foundation finds a structural mismatch between high unemployment and unfilled digital posts, with shortages worst in software development, networking and cybersecurity. It reports that most digital graduates concentrate in IT management and digital design rather than the fields employers want most, and that no single body is accountable for steering the skills pipeline from training through to jobs.

Why it matters for AHEAD: The report is a direct call to Wits AHEAD's fourth pillar, AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions: it shows that producing more graduates is not enough unless training is matched to real-time labour market data and backed by stronger national coordination.

World Bank · Report, intergovernmental body

entry.title: Study at South African university frames AI and academic integrity as a governance problem
entry.summary:
A qualitative case study of 16 postgraduate public health students at a South African research-intensive university, by Stephen Mongwe, Geesje Van den Berg and Patience Kelebogile Mudau, found that students valued generative AI's usefulness but worried about overreliance, blurred authorship, data privacy and the erosion of critical thinking. Unequal access to digital resources and unclear institutional expectations shaped how students actually used AI, leading the authors to argue that academic integrity in the AI era is a systemic governance problem rather than a matter of detection alone.

Why it matters for AHEAD: The study backs Wits AHEAD's first pillar, generative AI in higher education, with evidence that assessment redesign, clear AI-integrated integrity policies and shared institutional accountability matter more than catching students out, a lesson that applies well beyond this one university.

Journal of Ethics in Higher Education · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Wits professor urges South Africa to build its own AI capacity, not just import it
entry.summary:
Speaking to SAnews in San Jose during President Cyril Ramaphosa's AI delegation visit to Silicon Valley, Wits computer science professor Benjamin Rosman, who chairs the advisory panel revising South Africa's national AI policy, said South Africa must build its own AI capacity rather than depend on developments elsewhere. He pointed to the country's existing universities, researchers and entrepreneurs as a foundation, and warned that decisions made in the next two to five years, on risks such as job disruption and cybercrime, will shape the country for decades.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar six, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, and pillar four, AI and graduate employability, Rosman's call for home grown AI capacity, built on existing university expertise, matches Wits AHEAD's own mission to strengthen Global South capability rather than simply importing AI tools designed elsewhere.

SAnews (South African Government News Agency) · Government news agency report

entry.title: Universitat Jaume I video: UCL researcher Melissa Bond on AI in higher education teaching and research
entry.summary:
In a video published by Spain's Universitat Jaume I, Melissa Bond of University College London discusses how generative AI and large language models are changing classroom teaching and research in higher education. Recorded at the EDUTEC 2026 international conference in Castelló, the interview covers responsible AI use in evidence synthesis, guided by the RAISE principles, and how AI-assisted review tools can speed up systematic reviews while leaving more time for policy impact.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar one, generative AI in higher education, and pillar five, analytics and data for education systems, Bond's call for evidence-guided, responsible AI adoption echoes Wits AHEAD's own insistence that AI tools in teaching and research be adopted with safeguards, not enthusiasm alone.

Universitat Jaume I (EDUTEC 2026 international conference) · University conference video

entry.title: US study builds a behavioural early warning system from ordinary online course clicks
entry.summary:
A study in Issues in Information Systems by researchers at Georgia College and State University in the United States built a behavioural early warning system from 32,593 students and more than 10.6 million clickstream interactions in the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset. Using four measures of how consistently, intensely and evenly students spaced their study sessions, a logistic regression model correctly flagged failing students 81 per cent of the time, reaching 62.6 per cent overall accuracy after just 30 days of data and 68.7 per cent by day 150. Moderately and steadily spread out study sessions were linked to success, while bursts of very high intensity study were linked to greater risk of failing.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar two, AI and predictive analytics for student success, retention and early warning, this behavioural early warning model, built from ordinary learning management system clicks rather than costly new instruments, offers Wits AHEAD a practical template for flagging at risk students early enough to intervene in large Global South online and blended courses.

Issues in Information Systems, Georgia College and State University · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Office for Students and Advance HE report says AI detection cannot be trusted to protect degree standards
entry.summary:
On 11 November 2026 the Office for Students and Advance HE published Making AI Work for Students, drawing on over 300 students and staff across more than 120 English higher education institutions surveyed between June and September 2026. It found that unsupervised assessments can often be completed to a high standard using generative AI, that detection tools do not reliably identify AI use, and that most institutions' AI approaches have grown from individual staff experimentation rather than senior leadership strategy. Training in AI literacy for students and staff remains patchy and largely optional.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar one, generative AI in higher education: teaching, assessment and integrity, this is a system wide evidence base rather than one university's policy, and its warning that detection cannot be relied on strengthens the case, which Wits AHEAD has long made, for redesigning assessment rather than policing it.

Office for Students and Advance HE · National regulator and sector body joint report

entry.title: Randomised trial finds course integrated AI tutor lowered grades and cut engagement for US undergraduates
entry.summary:
A randomised controlled trial of 2,379 undergraduates and 30 instructors at a large United States public university found that access to a course integrated generative AI tutor reduced final grades by 0.37 of a standard deviation and cut engagement with the learning management system by 0.90 of a standard deviation, compared with sections without access. The authors, led by Jing Liu and Tracy Sweet, report that estimated academic losses were greater for first generation students, and conclude the tutor displaced existing study activity rather than improving learning.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar one, generative AI in higher education, and pillar two, AI and predictive analytics for student success, this finding that an unguided AI tutor can widen gaps for first generation students is a caution Wits AHEAD takes seriously as it designs AI support for a Global South student body with its own access and preparation gaps.

IZA Institute of Labor Economics working paper by Jing Liu, Tracy Sweet and colleagues · Working paper, randomised controlled trial

entry.title: Google.org-funded AI Research Foundations programme begins training South African university lecturers
entry.summary:
The Google.org funded AI Research Foundations programme launched in South Africa on 9 November 2026 with a five day workshop for university lecturers at Stellenbosch University's Biomedical Research Institute, drawing academics from Stellenbosch, the University of Venda, the University of Mpumalanga, the University of the Free State and the University of the Western Cape. Delivered by the FATE Foundation and the African Institute for Mathematical Sciences South Africa on a curriculum built by Google DeepMind with University College London, the train the trainer programme aims to reach ten South African universities as part of a wider target of thirty universities across Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa, ultimately training 30,000 students.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar four, AI, graduate capability, employability and just transitions, a train the trainer model that equips lecturers rather than only students matters for how quickly South African universities can build durable AI research capacity rather than depending on one off workshops.

Innovation Village (AI Africa Intelligence digest), reporting the Google.org-funded AI Research Foundations launch · Technology news digest report on a philanthropically funded university training programme

entry.title: Guiding students to use an AI tutor well matters more than just giving them access, Chilean field experiment finds
entry.summary:
A randomised field experiment in undergraduate econometrics at a Chilean university, reported in an IZA Institute of Labor Economics working paper by Sebastian Gallegos of Universidad Adolfo Ibanez, tested a course specific AI study assistant across seven sections. Simply encouraging students to adopt the tool before the midterm raised awareness and use but made no difference to midterm scores, while guiding students to use it as a tutor, working through concepts step by step, before the final exam raised final exam performance by 0.22 standard deviations and perceived usefulness by 0.38 standard deviations, concentrated in open response questions.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar one, generative AI in higher education, the finding that guidance on how to use an AI assistant matters more than simply giving students access speaks directly to how Wits AHEAD designs AI supported teaching across the Global South.

IZA Institute of Labor Economics working paper by Sebastian Gallegos (Universidad Adolfo Ibanez) · Working paper, randomised field experiment

entry.title: Universities clone lecturers as AI avatars to extend teaching support

category.term: United Kingdom, United States and Australia

entry.summary:
Imperial Business School, Harvard Business School, Columbia University's School of Nursing and the University of Illinois's Gies College of Business are among a growing number of institutions building AI avatars of lecturers to extend teaching support beyond the classroom. Imperial began cloning faculty in 2024, starting with Professor David Shrier, so that distant and overseas students can reach a digital version of their lecturer at any hour; Gies College of Business now has about a dozen faculty with voice or video clones, updated by editing a script rather than re-recording a lecture. A pilot at the University of Northampton found students valued the access but worried about losing personal connection, and recommended configurable guardrails that route sensitive questions to a human member of staff.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's first pillar, generative AI in higher education, this shows the technology moving from chatbots to faculty likenesses with a lecturer's own voice; the guardrails these universities are already building in, among them human escalation for sensitive questions, point to lessons for any institution considering the same step.

Times Higher Education · Established press

entry.title: AI-detection tools keep flagging non-native English writers as cheats, researchers warn

category.term: Global, with examples from South Africa and the Philippines

entry.summary:
Writing in University World News, health informatics scholar Davis Austria warns that the AI-detection tools many universities rely on routinely misclassify the English of non-native speakers as AI-generated, citing research on writers from South Africa and the Philippines whose sentence patterns are mistaken for machine output. A 2026 study that tested detectors on master's theses by non-native English speakers found Turnitin flagged none of the fully AI-generated papers correctly while Pangram performed best, and an earlier study found that simply introducing spelling errors cut one detector's accuracy from 39.5% to 12.9%. In one case reviewed by England and Wales's Office of the Independent Adjudicator, a student's explanation that they had used Google to find synonyms, because English was not their first language, was treated as an admission of AI use and led to a grade penalty across their whole degree, a decision the ombudsman later found unsupported by the record.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's sixth pillar, equity in responsible AI, this is a sharp reminder that detection tools trained mainly on native English writing can penalise the Global South's own students hardest, and that a detector's score should prompt a conversation with a student rather than stand alone as proof.

University World News · Established press (commentary citing peer-reviewed research)

entry.title: East African Community adopts a regional AI strategy with universities at its centre

category.term: East Africa (Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan)

entry.summary:
Education ministers of the East African Community adopted a regional Artificial Intelligence Strategy at the 21st Sectoral Council meeting in Kampala, held from 27 to 31 October 2026, approving a foundational AI module for undergraduates in any field of study and a Regional Artificial Intelligence Network of Universities to coordinate AI teaching, research and innovation across the bloc. The Inter-University Council for East Africa must now draw up a framework to implement the module, ready institutions may pilot it, and three new instruments will guide teacher education, institutional policy and codes of conduct. On the Commonwealth's new Ayre AI readiness index, Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and Rwanda all scored below the readiness benchmark, with Kenya highest at 48.7 out of 100.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For Wits AHEAD's fifth pillar, analytics and data for education systems, this is one of the first regional blocs turning an AI strategy into a concrete university curriculum mandate and a shared network, rather than leaving each institution to act alone.

TechTrendsKE · Intergovernmental body (reported by specialist technology press)

entry.title: Google DeepMind and Fab AI to build open AI tools for African teachers
entry.summary:
Google DeepMind and the non-profit Fab AI, jointly funded by Google.org and the Gates Foundation, will work with local innovators in Kenya, Ghana and South Africa to build teacher tools on open Gemma models for lesson planning, diagnostic feedback and coaching, running on low-cost devices and adapted to local languages and curricula. The first phase aims to reach up to 500 teachers and 15,000 pupils, with the resulting datasets, evaluation suites and models shared openly so others can adapt them. A separate, free Google AI Educator Series is also expanding across the region, starting in South Africa with the South African Council for Educators before reaching Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana in 2027.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar three, AI and analytics in STEM and teacher education, open models built for local languages and curricula matter more for scale across the Global South than any single licensed tool.

entry.title: Universities push AI firms to be more transparent on costs
entry.summary:
The UK sector body Jisc, backed by Universities UK and Guild HE, has published a call to suppliers asking AI companies to agree standard terms on pricing, usage metrics and governance before institutions sign contracts. Its six expectations include warning suppliers against uncontrolled cost escalation, continued access to specific model versions where teaching or research needs reproducibility, and protection from disruptive changes or supplier lock-in. Jisc's director of licensing, Caren Milloy, said institutions need confidence that they remain in control of their costs, choices and risks as adoption scales.

Why it matters for AHEAD: For pillar six, responsible AI, ethics, equity and policy, this is a rare case of universities acting collectively to set terms with AI vendors, rather than each institution negotiating alone.
